summary.text: Expressing successive binomial coefficients as the previous ones times \(U_x=\prod_{p\nmid k}(1+x p^r/k)\), pairing \(k\) with \(p^r-k\) and evaluating reciprocal power sums gives \(U_2^2-1=3(U_1^2-1)\) and enough divisibility of \(U_1-1\); together with the divisibility of \(6\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}^2-27\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}}\), this makes the desired difference vanish.  For \(r=2\) the pairing is sharpened using fourth-power reciprocal sums when \(p\ge7\), while \((p,r)=(3,2),(5,2)\) are settled by direct modular computations; the \(p=3\) argument otherwise uses the corresponding one-power-weaker product estimate compensated by divisibility modulo \(3^4\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 3\) and every \(r\geq2\),
\[
 a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
All fractions used below have denominators prime to \(p\), and are therefore interpreted in the relevant residue ring \(\mathbb Z/p^N\mathbb Z\).

## 1. A product expression for consecutive binomial coefficients

Put
\[
 C_c(s)=\binom{c p^s}{p^s}\qquad(c\geq1),
\]
and, for \(q=p^s\), let
\[
 S(p,q)=\{k:1\leq k\leq q,\ p\nmid k\}.
\]
For an integer \(x\geq0\), define
\[
 U_x(q)=\prod_{k\in S(p,q)}\left(1+\frac{xq}{k}\right).
\]
The modulus in which this product is considered will always be clear from context.

We first establish the exact quotient identity
\[
 C_c(s)=C_c(s-1)U_{c-1}(p^s)                         \tag{1}
\]
in every ring \(\mathbb Z/p^N\mathbb Z\), for \(s\geq1\).

Indeed,
\[
 (p^s)!\binom{cp^s}{p^s}
 =\prod_{k=1}^{p^s}((c-1)p^s+k).
\]
Split both sides into factors indexed by multiples of \(p\) and factors indexed by numbers not divisible by \(p\). The product of the multiples of \(p\) in \(1,\dots,p^s\) is
\[
 p^{p^{s-1}}(p^{s-1})!,
\]
while the corresponding factors in the numerator are
\[
 \prod_{\ell=1}^{p^{s-1}}\bigl((c-1)p^s+p\ell\bigr)
 =p^{p^{s-1}}\prod_{\ell=1}^{p^{s-1}}\bigl((c-1)p^{s-1}+\ell\bigr).
\]
After cancellation of these common factors and use of the same factorial identity at level \(s-1\), one obtains the integer identity
\[
 C_c(s)\prod_{k\in S(p,p^s)}k
 =C_c(s-1)\prod_{k\in S(p,p^s)}((c-1)p^s+k).
\]
The first product is prime to \(p\), hence invertible modulo every power of \(p\). Dividing by it gives (1).

For the two binomial coefficients in the theorem, write, in
\(R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z\),
\[
 A=C_3(r),\quad A_0=C_3(r-1),\quad
 B=C_2(r),\quad B_0=C_2(r-1),
\]
and
\[
 u=U_2(p^r),\qquad v=U_1(p^r).
\]
Then (1) says
\[
 A=A_0u,\qquad B=B_0v.                               \tag{2}
\]

## 2. Pairing the factors

The map
\[
 k\longmapsto q-k,
 \qquad q=p^r,
\]
is an involution of \(S(p,q)\). It has no difficulty at the endpoints: if \(p\nmid k\), then \(k\ne q\), so \(1\leq q-k\leq q\), and since \(p\mid q\), also \(p\nmid(q-k)\).

Pairing the two copies of \(U_x(q)\), one indexed by \(k\) and the other reindexed by \(q-k\), gives
\[
 U_x(q)^2
 =\prod_{k\in S(p,q)}
 \left(1+\frac{x(x+1)q^2}{k(q-k)}\right).            \tag{3}
\]
To check the individual factor, expand the left side:
\[
 \left(1+\frac{xq}{k}\right)
 \left(1+\frac{xq}{q-k}\right).
\]
Since
\[
 \frac1k+\frac1{q-k}=\frac q{k(q-k)},
\]
the sum of the two linear terms and the quadratic term is
\[
 \frac{xq^2}{k(q-k)}+\frac{x^2q^2}{k(q-k)}
 =\frac{x(x+1)q^2}{k(q-k)}.
\]

Suppose first that \(r\geq3\). In the ring \(R\), the product of any two perturbation terms in (3) contains \(q^4=p^{4r}\), which is zero because
\[
 4r\geq3r+3.
\]
Consequently the product in (3) truncates after its linear part:
\[
 U_x(q)^2
 =1+x(x+1)q^2\sum_{k\in S(p,q)}\frac1{k(q-k)}.       \tag{4}
\]
Using \(x=2\) and \(x=1\), whose coefficients are respectively \(6\) and \(2\), gives
\[
 u^2-1=3(v^2-1).                                     \tag{5}
\]
This is the first key relation.

## 3. Reciprocal sums and the size of \(U_x-1\)

We require standard reciprocal-sum vanishings, which we now prove.

For \(m\geq1\), let
\[
 H_m(p^j)=\sum_{z\in(\mathbb Z/p^j\mathbb Z)^\times}z^{-m}.
\]
Multiplication of the unit group by \(2\) permutes it. Therefore
\[
 H_m(p^j)=2^{-m}H_m(p^j),
\]
so
\[
 (2^m-1)H_m(p^j)=0.                                  \tag{6}
\]
For \(m=1\), the factor \(2^m-1=1\), and hence
\[
 H_1(p^j)=0\quad(p\geq3).                             \tag{7}
\]
For \(m=2\), (6) gives \(3H_2(p^j)=0\). Thus
\[
 H_2(p^j)=0\quad(p\geq5),                            \tag{8}
\]
because \(3\) is then a unit. For \(p=3\), it instead says that \(H_2(3^j)\) is divisible by \(3^{j-1}\). Finally, for \(m=4\), the factor is \(15\), so
\[
 H_4(p^j)=0\quad(p\geq7).                            \tag{9}
\]

The integers in \(S(p,p^j)\) are precisely the standard representatives of the units modulo \(p^j\). Inversion merely permutes the units. Hence (7)--(9) apply equally to sums of \(k^{-1},k^{-2},k^{-4}\) over this set.

We next strengthen the first reciprocal sum for \(p\geq5\). Work modulo \(p^{2r}\), and set
\[
 T_1=\sum_{k\in S(p,p^r)}\frac1k,
 \qquad
 T_2=\sum_{k\in S(p,p^r)}\frac1{k^2}.
\]
Reindexing by \(k\mapsto p^r-k\), and using
\[
 \frac1k+\frac1{p^r-k}=\frac{p^r}{k(p^r-k)},         \tag{10}
\]
gives
\[
 2T_1=p^r\sum_k\frac1{k(p^r-k)}.
\]
Modulo \(p^{2r}\), one also has
\[
 \frac{p^r}{k(p^r-k)}\equiv-\frac{p^r}{k^2}.         \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, after bringing the two sides together and using (10), the difference contains \(p^{2r}\). Thus
\[
 2T_1=-p^rT_2.
\]
By (8), \(T_2\equiv0\pmod {p^r}\), so the right side vanishes modulo \(p^{2r}\). Since \(2\) is a unit,
\[
 T_1\equiv0\pmod {p^{2r}}\qquad(p\geq5).             \tag{12}
\]
Together, (8) and (12) imply
\[
 \sum_k k^{-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^{2r}},\qquad
 \sum_k k^{-2}\equiv0\pmod {p^r}.                  \tag{13}
\]

Expand
\[
 U_x(p^r)=\prod_k\left(1+\frac{xp^r}{k}\right)

after reduction modulo \(p^{3r}\). The degree-one term is zero by the first congruence in (13), since it is multiplied by \(p^r\). The sum of the degree-two terms is also zero: because \(2\) is invertible,
\[
 2\sum_{i<j}\frac1{ij}
 =\left(\sum_i\frac1i\right)^2-\sum_i\frac1{i^2},
\]
and both terms on the right vanish modulo \(p^r\); multiplication by \(p^{2r}\) then kills the degree-two contribution modulo \(p^{3r}\). Every term of degree at least three visibly contains \(p^{3r}\). Therefore
\[
 U_x(p^r)\equiv1\pmod {p^{3r}}
 \qquad(p\geq5).                                     \tag{14}
\]

For \(p=3\), the same argument loses one power of \(3\). From (6),
\[
 \sum_k k^{-2}\equiv0\pmod {3^{r-1}}.
\]
Applying the pairing calculation (10)--(11) modulo \(3^{2r-1}\) gives
\[
 \sum_k k^{-1}\equiv0\pmod {3^{2r-1}}.
\]
Consequently the linear and quadratic terms in the expansion vanish modulo \(3^{3r-1}\), and all terms of degree at least three contain \(3^{3r}\). Hence, for \(r\geq2\),
\[
 U_x(3^r)\equiv1\pmod {3^{3r-1}}.                    \tag{15}
\]

Let \(\delta=v-1\). For \(p\geq5\), (14) says \(p^{3r}\mid\delta\), so \(\delta^2=0\) modulo \(p^{3r+3}\), since \(6r\geq3r+3\). For \(p=3\), (15) says \(3^{3r-1}\mid\delta\), and again \(\delta^2=0\) modulo \(3^{3r+3}\), because
\[
 2(3r-1)\geq3r+3\quad(r\geq2).
\]
Thus in all cases under consideration,
\[
 (v-1)^2=0\quad\text{in }R.                          \tag{16}
\]
Combining (5) with
\[
 v^2-1=(v-1)^2+2(v-1)=2(v-1)
\]
gives, whenever (5) is available,
\[
 u^2-1=6(v-1).                                        \tag{17}
\]

## 4. The auxiliary coefficient

We next show that
\[
 K:=6A_0^2-27B_0                                    \tag{18}
\]
has enough divisibility to annihilate \(v-1\).

For \(p\geq5\), (14), reduced modulo \(p^3\), and the quotient identity (1) show inductively that
\[
 C_c(s)\equiv C_c(0)=c\pmod {p^3}.                   \tag{19}
\]
Therefore
\[
 K\equiv6\cdot3^2-27\cdot2=0\pmod {p^3}.             \tag{20}
\]
Since \(p^{3r}\mid(v-1)\), (20) yields
\[
 K(v-1)\equiv0\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.                     \tag{21}
\]

For \(p=3\), reduce (15) modulo \(3^4\). For every \(s\geq1\), repeated use of (1) gives
\[
 C_c(s)\equiv C_c(1)=\binom{3c}{3}\pmod {3^4}.
\]
Here
\[
 C_3(1)=\binom93=84,
 \qquad C_2(1)=\binom63=20.
\]
Thus, when \(r\geq3\) (so \(r-1\geq1\)),
\[
 K\equiv6\cdot84^2-27\cdot20=41796=516\cdot81
 \equiv0\pmod {3^4}.                                \tag{22}
\]
Together with \(3^{3r-1}\mid(v-1)\), this again gives (21), now with \(p=3\), because \(4+(3r-1)=3r+3\).

## 5. Completion for \(r\geq3\)

Using (2), the difference we want to prove zero in \(R\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A^2-27B-(A_0^2-27B_0)
 &=A_0^2(u^2-1)-27B_0(v-1)\\
 &=\bigl(6A_0^2-27B_0\bigr)(v-1),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality uses (17). This is zero by (21). This proves the theorem for every \(r\geq3\), both for \(p=3\) and for \(p\geq5\).

## 6. The case \(r=2\) for \(p\geq7\)

For \(r=2\), the simple truncation used in (4) is not sufficient, because \(q^4=p^8\) need not vanish modulo \(p^9\). We refine it.

In \(R=\mathbb Z/p^9\mathbb Z\), set
\[
 g_k=\frac{p^4}{k(p^2-k)}.
\]
The paired product (3) is \(\prod_k(1+c g_k)\), with \(c=x(x+1)\). Every product of three \(g_k\)'s contains \(p^{12}\), hence vanishes modulo \(p^9\). We show that the total quadratic contribution also vanishes.

First,
\[
 \sum_k g_k^2
 =p^8\sum_k\frac1{k^2(p^2-k)^2}.
\]
Modulo \(p\), one has \(p^2-k\equiv-k\), so the remaining sum is
\[
 \sum_k k^{-4},
\]
which is zero by (9). Therefore \(\sum g_k^2=0\pmod {p^9}\).

Second,
\[
 \sum_k g_k=p^4\sum_k\frac1{k(p^2-k)}.
\]
Modulo \(p\), the latter sum is \(-\sum k^{-2}=0\), by (8). Hence \(\sum g_k\) is divisible by \(p^5\), and its square is zero modulo \(p^9\). Since
\[
 2\sum_{i<j}g_ig_j
 =\left(\sum_i g_i\right)^2-\sum_i g_i^2

a nd \(2\) is invertible, all quadratic terms vanish. Thus
\[
 \prod_k(1+c g_k)=1+c\sum_k g_k.
\]
Applying this with \(c=6\) and \(c=2\) once again yields
\[
 u^2-1=3(v^2-1).
\]
The general estimate (14) gives \(v-1\equiv0\pmod {p^6}\), so \((v-1)^2=0\pmod {p^9}\), and hence (17) follows. Also (20) gives \(p^3\mid K\). Therefore \(K(v-1)\) is divisible by \(p^9\), and the same final algebra as in Section 5 proves the result for \(r=2\) and \(p\geq7\).

The restriction \(p\geq7\) in this argument occurs exactly in the fourth-power sum: multiplication by \(2\) shows that \(15H_4=0\), and \(15\) is a unit precisely for primes other than \(3\) and \(5\).

## 7. The two remaining cases

Only \((p,r)=(3,2)\) and \((5,2)\) remain. They are direct finite calculations.

For \(p=3\),
\[
 \binom{27}{9}=4686825,\quad \binom{18}{9}=48620,
 \quad \binom93=84,\quad \binom63=20.
\]
The difference between the two corresponding values of \(a\) is
\[
 21966327261369=3^9\cdot1116005043.
\]
Thus the required congruence holds modulo \(3^9\).

For \(p=5\),
\[
 \binom{75}{25}=52588547141148893628,
 \quad \binom{50}{25}=126410606437752,
\]
and
\[
 \binom{15}{5}=3003,
 \qquad \binom{10}{5}=252.
\]
The difference between the two corresponding values of \(a\) is
\[
 2765555290416839473031163791322076171875
 =5^9\cdot1415964308693421810191955861156903.
\]
Hence the congruence also holds modulo \(5^9\).

We have covered \(r=2\) for \(p=3\), \(p=5\), and \(p\geq7\), and \(r\geq3\) for \(p=3\) and \(p\geq5\). These cases exhaust all primes \(p\geq3\) and all integers \(r\geq2\). Therefore
\[
 \boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}}.
\]
